exit.q: Big question: how do you find the interval from -5 to 4?

lessons.unit: Unit 2: The four operations
lessons.title: Adding and subtracting large numbers
objectives: Add and subtract numbers with up to 7 digits using written methods
Choose appropriate methods and check by estimating

keywords.def: writing numbers one above the other with place values lined up
swap 1 of one place for 10 of the place to its right
an approximate answer found by rounding

teach.heading: Column addition, 7 digits
teach.note: Continue: thousands 8 + 9 = 17, write 7 carry 1; ten thousands 6 + 7 + 1 = 14, write 4 carry 1; hundred thousands 4 + 5 + 1 = 10, write 0 carry 1; millions 2 + 1 + 1 = 4. Answer 4,047,773. Estimate: 2,500,000 + 1,600,000 = 4,100,000.

teach.heading: Column subtraction
teach.note: Work through the exchanges one place at a time, starting from the first non-zero digit to the left of each zero. Check using the inverse: 3,182,526 + 2,847,689 = 6,030,215.

teach.heading: Estimate to check
teach.note: Ask: would 40,477,730 pass the estimate check? Using rounding spots place value errors quickly.

teach.heading: Choose the method
bullets: Use mental methods when numbers are friendly.
Use columns for large messy numbers.
teach.note: Show 5,000,000 - 1 = 4,999,999 mentally. Ask pupils to decide, calculation by calculation, which method is quickest and safest.

independent: A city had 3,482,600 people in 2010 and 4,157,900 in 2020. How many more people lived there in 2020?
Use the inverse operation to check that 6,403,200 - 2,555,900 = 3,847,300.
A charity collected £1,250,000 in year 1, £980,500 in year 2 and £1,375,250 in year 3. How much altogether?
lessons.homework: Write four large addition and subtraction calculations about populations, check each with an estimate and the inverse.
lessons.send: SEND: place value columns, digit cards, coloured exchanges. EAL: model 'carry' and 'exchange'. Stretch: calculations with decimals or three numbers.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: The four operations
lessons.title: Short division
objectives: Divide up to a 4-digit number by a 1-digit number using short division
Interpret remainders

keywords.def: the amount left over after dividing

starter: Write the multiples of 7 up to 70.

teach.heading: The bus stop method
bullets: Divide each digit in turn, from the left.
Write the answer above the line.
Carry the remainder to the next digit.
teach.note: Draw the bus stop shape on the board. Remind pupils to use known times tables. Ask: why do we start at the left?
Check with the inverse: 1,358 x 4 = 5,432. Show how the remainder becomes the tens digit of the next number.

teach.heading: Remainders
teach.note: Work 4,615 ÷ 6: 46 ÷ 6 = 7 r 4; 41 ÷ 6 = 6 r 5; 55 ÷ 6 = 9 r 1. The remainder after the last digit is the remainder of the answer.

teach.heading: Zeros and small digits
bullets: When a digit is smaller than the divisor, write 0.
teach.note: Example with a zero: 2,412 ÷ 4 = 603. Pupils often leave out the 0 and write 63.

practice: Work out 3,509 ÷ 7 and write the remainder.
independent: 1,840 sweets are shared equally between 8 classes. How many does each class get?
exit: Work out 5,234 ÷ 4 and give the remainder.
lessons.homework: Make up four short division questions with a 4-digit number and a 1-digit divisor and solve them with checks.
lessons.send: SEND: times tables grid, partially completed bus stops. EAL: pre-teach divide/divisor/remainder. Stretch: divide larger numbers by 11 or 12 using short division.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: The four operations
lessons.title: Interpreting remainders
objectives: Express remainders as fractions, decimals or by rounding
Choose how to deal with a remainder in context

keywords.def: the amount left over after dividing exactly as far as possible
go to the next whole number
ignore the remainder and keep the whole number

starter: Say Bismillah. Work out 59 ÷ 4 with a remainder.

teach.heading: A remainder as a fraction
bullets: The remainder is 3 out of 4, so 14 3/4.
teach.note: The remainder becomes the numerator and the divisor becomes the denominator. Check that 0.75 = 3/4.

teach.heading: Share £75 between 6
teach.note: Continue the division with a decimal point: 75.0 ÷ 6 = 12.5. Link to money: always give two decimal places. £250 shared equally between 8 families gives £31.25 each.

teach.heading: Round up
bullets: 9 buses leave 6 behind, so we need 10 buses.
teach.note: Ask: would you really leave 6 pupils behind? Context decides. Rounding up is needed when everyone must be included.

teach.heading: Round down
bullets: Cakes are sold in boxes of 12. We have 90 cakes.
teach.note: Rounding down is needed when only complete groups count. Discuss: the 6 leftover cakes could be sold separately, but they do not fill a box.

practice: Write 47 ÷ 5 with the remainder as a fraction and as a decimal.
Eggs come in boxes of 6. How many boxes are needed for 100 eggs?
£90 is shared equally between 8 people. How much does each get?
independent: Give the answer as a mixed number and decimal: 26 ÷ 4; 41 ÷ 8; 99 ÷ 5.
A teacher needs 1 chair for each of 135 pupils. Chairs are stacked in 8s. How many stacks are needed?
£250 of sadaqah is shared equally between 8 families. How much does each receive?
For each, write whether to round up or down: seats on a bus for 74 people (bus holds 20); posters made from 74 m of paper (each uses 20 m).
exit: Write 38 ÷ 5 as a mixed number and decimal.
Buses hold 30 people. 100 people need transport. How many buses?
lessons.homework: Write three word problems whose answers need a remainder to be rounded up, rounded down or written as a fraction.
lessons.send: SEND: bar models and worked examples. EAL: pre-teach remainder/share/equally. Stretch: remainders in division by 2-digit numbers.

lessons.title: Bridge: order of operations
lessons.bigQuestion: Why must everyone agree on the order of operations?
objectives: To understand why we need an agreed order of operations
successCriteria: All: multiply and divide before adding and subtracting
Most: work out brackets first

lessons.crossCurricular: Computing: programming languages follow the order of operations

hook.text: Two pupils work out 3 + 4 × 5. One gets 35, the other 23. Who is right, and why does it matter?
hook.a: 23: multiply before adding. Without an agreed order, the same calculation would give different answers.

islamicLink.text: Muslim mathematicians such as al-Khwarizmi (الخوارزمي) in 9th-century Baghdad wrote rules for working with calculations; the word 'algebra' comes from his book title (al-jabr, الجَبْر).

pictures.alt: A page from al-Khwarizmi's book on calculation
A column addition set out on squared paper

teach.heading: The order
teach.note: Spoken: brackets, then multiply and divide, then add and subtract.

independent.q: Stretch: use 2, 3, 4 and 5 once each with any operations and brackets to make 24.

exit.q: Big question: why does the order of operations matter?
exit.a: So that everyone gets the same answer to the same calculation

lessons.homework: Bridge check: 8 order of operations questions and 2 'add the brackets' puzzles.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Order of operations, factors and problem solving
lessons.title: Multi-step problem solving
objectives: Solve multi-step problems using all four operations
Choose and check methods in context

keywords.def: a problem that needs more than one calculation
a diagram using bars to show the parts and whole of a problem
the opposite operation used to check

teach.heading: Four steps
bullets: Plan: which operations, in what order?
teach.note: Display the four steps. Ask pupils to underline the question and circle the numbers. Remind them to write units in the answer.

teach.heading: A building fund
bullets: Group A gave £25,350, group B gave £31,275.

teach.heading: Boxes and sharing
teach.note: Check: 72 x 12 = 864. Ask pupils whether the answer is reasonable: 12 families, 72 each, about 800 altogether.

teach.heading: Coaches and empty seats
teach.note: Start from the question 'how many seats are empty?' and work backwards to what you need to find first. Compare with a different problem where the 15 is given.

practice: A school buys 45 packs of 120 pencils and gives out 3,850. How many are left?
A mosque collects £4,500 on Friday and £3,750 on Saturday. This is shared equally among 5 projects. How much per project?
A train carries 1,248 passengers in 8 carriages. Each carriage has an equal number. How many in 3 carriages?
independent: A baker makes 24 trays of 36 buns. She sells 700. How many buns are left?
A fundraiser aims for £120,000. Week 1: £48,750. Week 2: £35,600. How much more is needed?
A coach trip costs £1,260 in total. 28 pupils share the cost equally. How much per pupil?
Write your own two-step problem using 18, 45 and 12 and solve it, showing a check.
exit: There are 36 boxes with 24 pencils in each. 150 pencils are used. How many are left?
£3,600 is shared equally between 15 people. How much each?

lessons.title: Metric measures
lessons.bigQuestion: Why is the metric system easy to convert?
objectives: To understand how metric units are related by powers of 10
successCriteria: All: name metric units of length, mass and capacity
Most: know how they are related (10, 100, 1,000)
Some: choose sensible units
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: measuring in experiments
lessons.smsc: Moral: fair measuring in trade

hook.text: Why do you think almost every country uses metres and kilograms rather than their own units?
hook.a: Metric units are linked by 10, 100 and 1,000, so converting is easy and everyone can trade fairly.

islamicLink.text: Allah commands: establish the weight with justice and do not make the balance short (Qur'an 55:9). Accurate measuring and converting are part of honest trade.

pictures.alt: Kitchen scales showing grams
A measuring jug marked in millilitres
A ruler with centimetre and millimetre marks

teach.heading: The links
teach.note: Ask: how many mm in 1 m? (1,000).

check.q: Which is the most sensible mass for an apple?

practice.model: Teacher: 1 kg = 1,000 g, so 3.5 kg = 3,500 g.

practice.q: Best unit for the length of a room?

independent.q: Core: 2,450 ml in litres; 4 km in m; 6 cm in mm
independent.model: Teacher: 1 l = 1,000 ml, so 2,450 ml = 2.45 l.

independent.q: Extend: order 0.8 kg, 750 g, 1.2 kg
Stretch: a recipe needs 1.25 kg flour. You have three 400 g bags. Enough?

exit.a: 1.5 km

exit.q: Big question: why is metric easy to convert?
exit.a: Units are linked by 10, 100 and 1,000, so we only move digits

lessons.homework: Find 5 food packets at home and convert each mass or volume to the other unit.
lessons.send: SEND: worked example kept on screen, concrete or pictorial first, reduced set. EAL: key word cards; stem 'First I ..., then I ...'. Stretch: convert mm to km.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Place value and the operations bridge; fractions; converting units
lessons.title: Convert metric measures
lessons.bigQuestion: How do we know whether to multiply or divide when converting?
objectives: To understand how to convert between metric units
successCriteria: All: convert from larger to smaller units by multiplying
Most: convert from smaller to larger units by dividing
Some: solve problems with mixed units
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: distances on maps in km and m
lessons.smsc: Social: sharing ingredients when cooking together

hook.text: Going from km to m, does the number get bigger or smaller? Why?
hook.a: Bigger: there are 1,000 m in each km, so we multiply.

pictures.alt: A tape measure showing metres and centimetres
Kilogram weights
A map scale bar marked in kilometres

independent.q: Core: 45 mm in cm; 3.08 km in m; 600 ml in l
Extend: a 2 l jug fills cups of 250 ml. How many cups?
Stretch: a 1.2 km route is walked 6 times a week. How many km in a week? In m?

exit.q: Big question: when do we multiply when converting?
exit.a: From a larger unit to a smaller unit, like km to m

lessons.homework: Spring half term: convert 10 measures from recipes and maps; times tables 5 minutes a day.
